article.headline: Bono's Reluctant Reckoning: Commerce as the Off-Ramp From Poverty
article.lede: In a 2022 New York Times Magazine interview tied to the release of his memoir, Bono told interviewer David Marchese that decades of working on African poverty had brought him somewhere he didn't expect: to the conclusion that markets, not redistribution, are the primary exit from extreme poverty. "The off-ramp out of extreme poverty," he said, "is, ugh, commerce, it's entrepreneurial capitalism." Alec Stapp, co-founder of the Institute for Progress, surfaced the quote — notable for its messenger as much as its message.
article.body:
The quote comes from a wide-ranging *New York Times Magazine* conversation published in October 2022, pegged to the release of Bono's memoir *Surrender: 40 Songs, One Story*. Asked about his decades of activism — debt cancellation, AIDS funding, the ONE Campaign — Bono offers something close to a quiet intellectual recantation. "I thought that if we just redistributed resources, then we could solve every problem," he says. "I now know that's not true." The "ugh" before "entrepreneurial capitalism" is doing essential work: he is not a convert in the ideological sense, but an activist who followed the evidence somewhere inconvenient.

His observation about Africa is the sharpest line. Bono notes that Africans themselves have told him they'd welcome more *globalization* — the integration of national economies through trade, investment, and the movement of goods — not less. This is an implicit rebuke of the aid-and-charity paradigm that long dominated Western development thinking: the idea that poverty could be solved by transferring resources from rich countries rather than by building the conditions for commerce. Zambian economist Dambisa Moyo made the same argument at length in *Dead Aid* (2009), and it remains a point of real agreement between African policymakers and market-friendly Western analysts.

The empirical case behind Bono's claim is strong, if not quite as clean as a single quote can capture. **The share of the world living in extreme poverty** — defined by the World Bank as surviving on less than $2.15 a day — fell from roughly 36 percent in 1990 to around 9 percent by 2022, lifting approximately 1.5 billion people. The largest gains came during the peak years of trade liberalization and were concentrated in China and South Asia, where export-led growth, not redistribution, was the principal engine. The World Bank's own assessment is direct: "Trade and global integration have raised incomes across the world, while dramatically cutting poverty."

The full interview, however, reveals a more textured position. When Marchese raises Thomas Piketty — the French economist whose *Capital in the Twenty-First Century* reignited global debate about inequality and wealth taxes — Bono does not dismiss him. "Capitalism is a wild beast," he says. "We need to tame it. But globalization has brought more people out of poverty than any other -ism." The truncated OCR fragment "If you read Thomas..." almost certainly leads into a reference to Piketty's more recent *A Brief History of Equality* (2022), which itself argues that living standards and rights have improved substantially — a data point Bono can use while still rejecting pure redistribution as the mechanism.

Stapp, whose Institute for Progress sits in a pro-growth, techno-optimist lane of Washington policy, is sharing the quote partly as a rhetorical instrument. A longtime left-leaning celebrity activist arriving at a market-friendly conclusion is useful to anyone trying to build a cross-ideological coalition around growth and progress. There is nothing Bono says that serious development economists haven't been debating for thirty years. The value here is the messenger — and the "ugh."

concepts.definition: Defined by the World Bank as living on less than $2.15 per day (in 2017 purchasing-power-parity terms). It is the standard international benchmark for the most severe deprivation and is used to track global progress on poverty reduction.

A form of market economy in which private individuals start and grow businesses as the primary mechanism of wealth creation and economic development, as opposed to state-directed investment or redistribution of existing resources. The term emphasizes the role of innovation and risk-taking, not just market exchange.

The deepening integration of national economies through cross-border trade, foreign direct investment, migration, and technology transfer. In development contexts it often refers specifically to export-led growth strategies, in which poor countries industrialize by producing goods for wealthier markets.

The view, dominant in Western development circles from roughly the 1960s through the 1990s, that poverty in the developing world is primarily a resource problem solvable by transferring money, food, or expertise from rich countries. Critics argue it crowds out domestic markets and creates dependency without building the institutions that sustain growth.

books.title: Surrender: 40 Songs, One Story
books.author: Bono
books.summary: Published in November 2022, Bono's memoir interweaves the story of U2's rise with his parallel life as a political activist — debt relief campaigns, the ONE Campaign, encounters with African heads of state and American presidents. The book is structured around forty U2 songs. The NYT Magazine interview that contains this quote was published the week before the book's release.

books.title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century
books.author: Thomas Piketty
books.summary: Published in French in 2013 and translated to English in 2014, Piketty's book argues that the rate of return on capital tends to exceed the rate of economic growth over time, causing wealth to concentrate. It became the central text of the redistribution-focused wing of progressive economics and is almost certainly the book Bono's interviewer raised in the context of the quote.

books.title: A Brief History of Equality
books.author: Thomas Piketty
books.summary: Published in 2022, this shorter Piketty work makes the counterintuitive argument that the long arc of history has actually bent toward equality — in rights, living standards, and access to education. It is more optimistic in tone than his earlier work, and Bono's truncated reference to reading "Thomas" in the NYT interview likely points here, since the book's progress-has-happened thesis is one Bono could cite in his own favor.

books.title: Dead Aid
books.author: Dambisa Moyo
books.summary: Published in 2009 by Zambian economist Dambisa Moyo, the book argues that Western foreign aid has done more harm than good in Africa — creating dependency, distorting markets, and undermining governance — and that trade, foreign direct investment, and access to capital markets are the real engines of African development. It caused significant controversy and remains a touchstone in debates about development strategy.

article.fact_check: Bono's core claim — that commerce and globalization have been the primary engine of poverty reduction — is directionally accurate and well-supported by World Bank and academic evidence. The framing, however, is a binary that most development economists would resist. The fastest poverty reductions, in China and South Asia, combined market integration with substantial state intervention, infrastructure investment, and social protection. Economists including Dani Rodrik and François Bourguignon argue that growth and redistribution are complements, not substitutes. Bono himself seems to sense this — "capitalism is a wild beast, we need to tame it" — but a single quote inevitably flattens that nuance.

poster_alecstapp.blurb: Alec Stapp is the co-founder of the Institute for Progress (IFP), a think tank focused on innovation and regulatory reform. He posts about housing policy, biomedical research, and infrastructure, often highlighting evidence-based policy proposals. On Bluesky, he has over 8,200 followers and his posts have garnered significant engagement.
